title: Delhi HC: Award Stamped in Gujarat Needs No Extra Duty Just for Enforcement in Delhi
meta_description: Delhi High Court rejects ONGC's objection that an arbitral award stamped under Gujarat law attracts fresh stamp duty merely on enforcement in Delhi.
case_name: Kirloskar Pneumatic Company Limited v. Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited
body: An arbitral award does not become a fresh taxable instrument every time its winner carries it across a state border to get it enforced. That, in short, is what the Delhi High Court held on 9 October 2026, rejecting the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation's objection that an award already stamped in Gujarat needed additional stamp duty before it could be enforced in Delhi.

The underlying dispute between Kirloskar Pneumatic Company Limited and ONGC had already gone through arbitration and a round of court scrutiny before this question even arose. The arbitral tribunal passed its award on 13 April 2023, corrected on 15 April 2023, in Kirloskar's favour. The award was signed in Ahmedabad and stamped under the Gujarat Stamp Act, 1958, which is the law that governs duty on instruments executed within that state. ONGC then took the award to the Commercial Court at Ankleshwar under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and succeeded in part, getting the interest component set aside and leaving Rs. 3,78,22,968 payable to Kirloskar under what remained of the award.

That left Kirloskar with a reduced but still-valid award to enforce, and it chose to do so in Delhi. ONGC resisted on a narrow but potentially expensive ground: that enforcement in Delhi triggered a fresh, differential stamp duty obligation under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 as it applies in the capital, over and above what had already been paid in Gujarat, and that Kirloskar's payment of that additional duty had come too late in any event. If ONGC were right, every award holder seeking to enforce an out-of-state award in Delhi would effectively face a second stamping exercise before enforcement could proceed, layering an additional cost and procedural step onto enforcement that the Arbitration Act does not obviously contemplate.

Justice Shukla did not accept that reading. The court held that an instrument executed and stamped in one state does not, merely by being brought into another state for enforcement, attract an obligation to pay differential stamp duty there as well, unless a specific statutory provision actually creates that liability. The mere fact that an instrument executed and stamped in one state is subsequently brought into another does not, without more, establish such an obligation. The judgment anchored this in the mechanics of the Stamp Act itself, treating execution, read together with Section 17 and the charging provisions in Section 2(12), as the event that triggers the duty, rather than treating each later act of presenting the instrument somewhere else as a fresh chargeable event.

ONGC's position was not frivolous on its own terms; stamp law genuinely does vary by state, and an instrument can sometimes attract further duty when it moves between jurisdictions in ways the relevant stamp statutes specifically provide for. What the court found missing here was exactly that kind of specific statutory hook. Without a provision in the Delhi-applicable stamp law that reaches an award already validly stamped elsewhere, ONGC's objection amounted to asking the court to infer a tax liability that no particular section actually imposed, and the court declined to do that inferential work on the government's behalf.

The ruling sits alongside a cluster of other 2026 Delhi High Court decisions on stamping and enforcement of arbitral awards, some of which have gone the other way on different facts, for instance by insisting that an insufficiently stamped award must be impounded before it can be enforced at all, or that a mere copy of an award cannot be stamped or impounded where the original is unavailable. Read together, these rulings are less about a single settled rule than about a court working through, award by award, where the line sits between genuine stamp-duty shortfalls that block enforcement and objections, like ONGC's here, that import an extra duty the statute never actually prescribed.

For award holders who litigate in one state and enforce in another, a routine pattern given how many arbitration clauses fix a seat different from where the paying party's assets sit, the practical message is that a State's own stamp duty, properly paid once at execution, should not need to be paid again just because enforcement proceedings are filed somewhere else. Parties resisting enforcement on stamp grounds will need to point to an actual statutory basis for any further duty they claim is owed, rather than relying on the simple fact that the award has crossed a state line.
why_it_matters: Award holders routinely enforce in a state different from where the award was signed and stamped, since arbitration seats and asset locations rarely match. This ruling confirms that crossing a state border does not, by itself, create a fresh stamp duty liability, cutting off a procedural objection that could otherwise delay or inflate the cost of enforcing out-of-state awards across India.
card_summary: Delhi High Court rejects ONGC's bid to demand fresh stamp duty on a Gujarat-stamped arbitral award merely because Kirloskar sought to enforce it in Delhi.
card_tip: Resisting enforcement of an out-of-state award on stamp duty grounds requires pointing to a specific statutory provision imposing fresh duty, not just the fact that the award crossed a state border.
verification_notes: The decision date (9 October 2026), bench, case number, the underlying award dates (13 and 15 April 2023), the Ankleshwar Commercial Court's Section 34 outcome, the Rs. 3,78,22,968 remaining principal, ONGC's differential-duty argument, and the court's holding and reasoning on Sections 17 and 2(12) of the Indian Stamp Act are drawn from LiveLawBiz's report, cross-checked against the Delhi High Court's own uploaded judgment file for the same case number, which is treated as the primary source. A related secondary report on a different, later Delhi High Court ruling (URC Construction v. Airports Authority of India) taking a stricter view on when duty becomes payable was not relied on for any fact stated here, since it concerns a separate case, and is mentioned only to flag that Delhi High Court rulings on award-stamping in 2026 have not all pointed the same way.
